name: cracked broken asphalt road crumbling into dirt, laid as a road network with crossroads and dead ends
label: wasteland_ruins/asphalt

surfaces.part: flat ground texture with asphalt road network (crossroads, dead ends) seen from above

answer.evidence: This is a seamless terrain tile that fills the full 176 px width across rows 0-191. It is a flat top-down ground texture of dirt with asphalt road strips. The roads have only thin dark 1-row edge shadows along their south edges, and there is no raised volume or vertical front face. The column scans show repeating texture bands with no front-face structure. As a terrain kind, it is a flat surface with no standing body.

styleAnswer.evidence: Measured facts: the candidate has 7 visible tones per tile, 0% near-flat coverage and 0% neutral dark edge pixels. That matches the paving reference's 7 tones and beats the grass reference's 3, so the numbers do not mark it as shallow. By eye the dirt ground carries speckle, crack lines and small pebbles in several brown tones, and the grey asphalt patches have per-chunk cobble dots with a darker blue-grey edge tint instead of a black line. The weaknesses are that the asphalt strips are fairly uniform, with 3-4 steps and little highlight/shadow definition. The dirt is a busy but repetitive noise with few distinct clumps, and the tiling is visible, with pebbles at regular intervals. The paving reference has crisper light edges and a clearer 5-6 step ramp. The candidate is acceptable but a bit thinner and flatter in the asphalt ramp, and the 'crumbling into dirt' transition is not shaded, only butted against the dirt. With doubt resolved toward failure, this is a marginal fail.

surfaces.part: dirt ground base with cracked asphalt road patches (crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends)

answer.evidence: This is a flat ground tile seen from above. The full 176x192 area is dirt and asphalt texture with no standing volume. The column scans show repeating texture runs and a 1-row dark crack line every 16 rows at x=88 (rows 35, 51, 67, ...). They show no front-edge line followed by a vertical face. The road patches carry only thin dark outline or shadow rows at their lower edges, about 1-2 rows, which do not form a front face of 3 or more rows. There is no receding side face, no ellipse and no roof. It is a terrain tile, so it reads as a flat top-down surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 7 visible tones per 16x16 tile, matching the paving reference (7) and well above the grass reference (3). Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references. The dirt has about 5 brown steps with speckle, grit, hairline cracks and small embedded stones. The asphalt strips have about 4-5 blue-grey steps with a per-stone cobbled grain and no flat areas of 5x5 or more. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted, with dark brown against the dirt and dark blue-grey against the asphalt. It does not have the near-black sticker look. Forms are separated mostly by value. The total palette is only 14 colours, a little thinner than the grass reference's 80 raw colours, but the visible tonal variety is equal or higher. Structurally it is at the same level as the references. The road edges are a little blotchy, and the crumbling transition into dirt is a bit soft, but this is a minor craft issue rather than a style failure.

surfaces.part: ground tile: dirt with cracked asphalt road network seen from above

answer.evidence: This is a full-bleed 176-wide terrain tile (rows 0-191 all at width 176), not a standing object. It shows a flat top-down ground texture: brown dirt with grey-blue asphalt road strips forming crossroads, a T-junction, and dead ends. The dark lines along the road bottoms (e.g. x=88 rows 35, 51, 67) are crack lines or road-edge shadows, not eave shadows. There is no front face and no vertical south face, so it reads as a flat top-down surface, which is normal for terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: Candidate: 7 visible tones per tile, equal to the paving reference (7) and above the grass (3). 0% near-flat coverage and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so outlines are tinted, not near-black. The soil reads as a brown ramp of about 4 steps with speckle, crack lines and small pebbles. The asphalt strips are blue-grey cobble-like clusters with a dark edge and little highlight, so they carry only about 3-4 steps. Against the paving reference's 5-6 steps with highlighted edges, the road is a little thinner. The road network (crossroads, dead ends) is present, but the asphalt looks like patchy cobble and shows little crumbling into the dirt. The soil is textured and not a flat fill. Overall it is close to the references but not clearly richer, so it is borderline. A careful artist would likely accept it beside the references, but the asphalt shading is shallow.

surfaces.part: cracked asphalt road network on dirt ground, seen from above

answer.evidence: This is a seamless ground tile: a full-bleed 176px-wide, 192-row field of dirt with asphalt road strips (crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends) drawn flat from above. The silhouette is a plain rectangle at width 176 for every row. The column scans show only repeating texture bands. There is no front-edge line, eave shadow, ellipse, or standing front face. The dark lower edges along the road strips are thin outlines, not a vertical face. As terrain, it is a flat top-down surface, so the view rules for standing objects do not apply.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 7 visible tones per tile, equal to the paving reference (7) and above the grass reference (3). Near-flat coverage is 0%. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines carry a tint. The dirt ground shows mottled brown grain, crack lines and pebble dots, so it is not a flat fill. The road segments are blue-grey cobble-like patches with a darker edge and a few lighter speckles. Their ramp is only about 3-4 steps, and the asphalt reads more like cobbles than cracked asphalt crumbling into dirt. The roads are also thin and sparse against the large dirt field, with no gradual crumbling transition at their edges. Shading depth and per-tile craft are a little below the Beodeul paving, though the measured facts match the references.
